messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samira, a 34-year-old divorced agricultural worker from a Middle Eastern family, came to treatment describing a steady narrowing of her life since she witnessed a traumatic event three years earlier in a field outside the town where she was working seasonally. One afternoon, while she and several others were harvesting, she saw a young mother across the road suddenly collapse after a confrontation nearby turned violent; the details she clung to were the baby’s cries, the way people on the roadside looked at one another before anyone moved, and the sense that ordinary conversation and ordinary faces could hide danger. In the weeks after, she found that certain conversation topics—anything about neighborhood conflict, family disputes, or what “really happened” in public—could pull her right back into that moment, and the sound of babies crying had the same effect, sharp and immediate, making her chest tighten as though she were again standing in the dust and heat with no way to make sense of what she had seen. People acting suspiciously, even small things like a man lingering too long near the irrigation shed or a coworker whispering while looking over her shoulder, made her body tense and her mind race toward the possibility that another bad event was about to unfold. Each of these reminders seemed to confirm her fear that the world was not reliably safe, and over time she came to believe that people were not what they seemed, that she had lost her faith in people and in life itself, and that she no longer belonged anywhere.

At first, Samira tried to outrun those reactions by forcing herself into order. She began cleaning and organizing repeatedly at home, wiping counters, folding clothes, lining up containers, and checking the same spaces again and again after work, telling herself that if her surroundings were neat enough and under control, her thoughts would settle. She also tried to push the memories out of her mind and made herself think only positive thoughts, repeating comforting phrases when the images came up, but the effort left her exhausted and tense. The more she scrambled to shut everything down, the more her mind seemed to return to the same suspicious details from that day, and the same fear that the world could turn dangerous without warning. In that way, the very strategies she relied on to manage the reminders seemed to deepen her distrust: every time she had to work so hard to keep herself together, it felt to her like proof that she could not trust her own mind, and that if she had to force positivity and bury the memories, then the truth underneath must be unbearable. She began to read other people’s glances as concealment, to see distance in conversation as evidence that she did not truly belong, and to feel that if she could not even speak honestly about what she had witnessed, there was nowhere in her life where she fit.

The practical consequences spread through her days. On the farm, Samira became cautious around coworkers she had once chatted with easily, especially if they spoke in hushed tones or mentioned family matters, and she noticed herself stepping away when a baby was brought to the worksite by a relative. She would tell herself to stay positive and keep moving, but that only made her more vigilant, scanning faces and rehearsing whether someone was acting suspiciously. When she got home, she cleaned until late at night, trying to wash away the feeling that danger had followed her there, yet each repeat of the ritual left her with the same bleak conclusion that nothing in people or in life could be counted on. Even in moments of temporary calm, she felt cut off from others and from any secure place in the world. She had been divorced shortly after these symptoms intensified, and though she did not describe the separation as the cause, she spoke about it as another confirmation that she no longer belonged anywhere.

Samira sought help after realizing that she was spending most of her waking hours either avoiding reminders, scrubbing or arranging things to feel in control, or bracing herself against the next intrusive image. What finally brought her in was the fear that the constant suspicion and effort were taking over her ability to work and to live with any ease. She said she was tired of feeling as though every suspicious glance, every upsetting conversation, and every baby’s cry could send her back to that roadside scene. What she most hoped for was a way to feel safe around other people again, and what frightened her most was that, without help, she might go on living as if she had no place in the world at all.
